reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: Rarest of the urea cycle disorders, caused by biallelic NAGS variants
NAGS makes N-acetylglutamate, the obligatory allosteric activator of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1, so its loss shuts down the first committed step of ureagenesis
Biochemically resembles CPS1 deficiency: hyperammonaemia with low/normal citrulline, low arginine and a characteristically low urine orotic acid
Presents as neonatal hyperammonaemic encephalopathy, or later with episodic hyperammonaemia and neurocognitive symptoms
The key distinguishing feature is its responsiveness to carglumic acid, a synthetic N-acetylglutamate analogue that restores CPS1 activity
Low or absent orotic aciduria helps separate proximal urea cycle defects (NAGS, CPS1) from OTC deficiency
Confirm with NAGS gene sequencing and by demonstrating a therapeutic response to carglumic acid
Acute management is emergency ammonia lowering (dialysis if needed) with carglumic acid, nitrogen scavengers, arginine and protein restriction
reference.pathophysiology: N-acetylglutamate synthase catalyses formation of N-acetylglutamate from glutamate and acetyl-CoA. N-acetylglutamate is the essential allosteric activator of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1 (CPS1), the enzyme that initiates the urea cycle by incorporating ammonia into carbamoyl phosphate. In NAGS deficiency the activator is not produced, so CPS1 remains inactive and the urea cycle cannot begin, leading to accumulation of ammonia. Because the block is at the very first step, downstream intermediates such as citrulline and arginine are low, and carbamoyl phosphate is not diverted into pyrimidine synthesis, so orotic acid excretion stays low (mirroring CPS1 deficiency and contrasting with OTC deficiency). Uniquely, the missing activator can be replaced pharmacologically by carglumic acid, which reactivates CPS1. Inheritance is autosomal recessive.
additionalDifferentials: Ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency (raised orotic acid, X-linked)
Fatty acid oxidation disorders with hyperammonaemia
additionalInvestigations: Urgent plasma ammonia during suspected crises
Plasma amino acids (low/normal citrulline, low arginine, raised glutamine)
Urine orotic acid (characteristically low, separating from OTC deficiency)
Blood gas showing respiratory alkalosis of hyperammonaemia
Documented biochemical response to a carglumic acid trial
Plasma acylcarnitines/organic acids to exclude secondary hyperammonaemia
redFlags: Neonatal hyperammonaemic coma requiring emergency ammonia removal
Rapidly rising ammonia with encephalopathy at any age
Decompensation triggered by catabolic illness, high protein load or surgery
Failure of ammonia to fall despite standard scavenger therapy (prompting carglumic acid)
reference.prognosis: NAGS deficiency is one of the few urea cycle disorders with a specific pharmacological treatment; with early diagnosis and carglumic acid therapy long-term metabolic control and outcome can be excellent, whereas delayed treatment of severe neonatal hyperammonaemia risks permanent neurological injury.
pitfalls: Not distinguishing NAGS from CPS1 deficiency and thereby missing a treatable disorder
Failing to trial carglumic acid, which is specifically effective in NAGS deficiency
Overlooking the low orotic acid clue that points to a proximal urea cycle defect
Delaying emergency ammonia lowering while awaiting confirmatory genetics
Assuming carglumic acid is equally effective in all urea cycle disorders
references: Scriver's Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease (OMMBID)
Saudubray, Inborn Metabolic Diseases: Diagnosis and Treatment
management: Give carglumic acid as specific disease-directed therapy, a synthetic N-acetylglutamate analogue that restores carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1 activity and can normalise ammonia
Institute a protein-restricted diet with adequate energy intake and essential amino-acid supplementation to limit ammonia generation

Treat acute hyperammonaemic crises by stopping protein intake, giving high-calorie glucose (with insulin if needed) to reverse catabolism, and intravenous carglumic acid with nitrogen-scavenger support
Escalate to haemodialysis or haemofiltration for severe or refractory hyperammonaemia to remove ammonia rapidly
Monitor plasma ammonia, amino acids and growth long term, and avoid catabolic triggers such as fasting, infection and the perioperative state
Provide an emergency regimen and sick-day plan with prompt hospital access during intercurrent illness

Offer genetic counselling and family screening given autosomal recessive inheritance, with antenatal or newborn diagnostic testing, and coordinate care through a metabolic medicine team with specialist dietetic input
